analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 28% and closes a tax-treaty loophole used by foreign-owned subsidiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the top corporate rate to 28% while tightening rules on foreign-owned subsidiaries never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower the top federal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 28%, cutting taxes for every large corporation and its shareholders. It pairs that cut with one narrow revenue-raiser: U.S. subsidiaries of foreign parent companies could no longer use tax treaties to pay lower withholding tax on deductible payments to related companies abroad. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders gain from the lower 28% top rate, which applies to all corporations, not just those harmed by the loophole closure [S2][S3]. The Treasury would gain some revenue from the provision that stops foreign-parent groups from using treaty rates to reduce tax on deductible related-party payments [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top marginal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 28%, including for personal service corporations, effective for tax years beginning after 2010 [S2][S3].

Prevents U.S. subsidiaries of foreign parent corporations from using tax-treaty rates to pay less withholding tax on deductible payments to related entities than would be owed if paid directly to the foreign parent [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury bears the revenue loss from the across-the-board corporate rate cut; only the narrow treaty provision raises revenue in return, so the bill is not self-financing [S3]. Reduced revenue eventually means higher deficits, higher other taxes, or smaller public spending.

drawbacks.text: The rate cut applies to all corporations, but the only offsetting revenue-raiser targets foreign-owned groups, so the bill cuts overall federal revenue by lowering the rate on all corporate income while recovering tax only from a narrow slice of foreign-parent payments [S3].

A seven-point cut in the top corporate rate primarily benefits the shareholders of large corporations, who are disproportionately higher-income households; the bill text contains no other pay-for [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The anti-treaty-abuse provision is a genuine fix worth supporting on its own. But the bill's headline is the rate cut, and the bill does not come close to paying for it: a 35% to 28% cut applies to the entire corporate tax base, while the offset touches only deductible related-party payments within foreign-controlled groups. As designed, it is mostly a tax cut for corporations with a small enforcement rider attached.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Djou (R-HI) introduced the bill on July 26, 2010, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law, on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and their shareholders kept the 35% corporate rate they would have paid 28% under the bill, and foreign-parent multinationals kept the treaty planning the bill would have shut down; no one in the public gained or lost because the bill never became law.

for.name: Rep. Charles K. Djou
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor

against.name: Rep. Sander Levin
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred to the committee; no action appears in the record beyond referral

sides.party_line_note: No votes or cosponsors exist to show the split; a lone House Republican sponsored the bill and it never moved in a Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.note: The bill cuts the top corporate rate from 35% to 28% across the board, a large tax benefit whose main beneficiaries are corporate shareholders. The offsetting revenue-raiser applies only to foreign-owned groups, so the cut is not paid for.

industries.industry: U.S. subsidiaries of foreign parent corporations
industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to use tax-treaty rates to lower withholding tax on deductible payments to related entities abroad. Closing the loophole raises revenue and serves ordinary taxpayers, which is why the industry's interest here runs against the bill.
The rate cut expressly applies to personal service corporations as well, lowering their top rate from 35% to 28%.
